‘Thank you, sir,’ the servant said, and left the room.

‘Now, Alan, we cannot waste a moment. This chest is heavy! I’ll carry it for you. Bring the other things.’ He spoke quickly and firmly, and Campbell felt himself under Dorian’s control. They went out together.

At the top landing Dorian produced the key and turned it in the lock. Then he stopped. His eyes grew troubled, and he shivered. ‘I don’t think I can go inside, Alan,’ he murmured.

‘That makes no difference to me. I don’t need you,’ Campbell replied coldly.

Dorian pushed the door halfway open. As it moved, he saw the face in his portrait grinning horribly in the sunlight. The torn curtain lay on the floor before it. He remembered that last night, for the first time in his life, he had forgotten to cover the terrible painting. He was about to rush forward, but shrank back with a shudder.

What were those disgusting red drops shining wetly on one of its hands, as though the canvas had sweated blood? How dreadful they were! For a moment they seemed even worse than the silent thing he knew lay across the table. Its twisted, misshapen shadow on the stained carpet showed him that it had not moved. It remained exactly where he had left it.

Taking a deep breath, he opened the door a little farther. With his eyes half shut and his head turned aside, he hurried in, determined not to look at the dead man even once. He bent down, picked up the gold-and-purple curtain, and threw it over the portrait.

He stopped there, afraid to turn around, staring at the complicated pattern in front of him. Behind him he heard Campbell bringing in the heavy chest, the irons, and the other things he had asked for to perform his dreadful task. Dorian began wondering whether Campbell and Basil Hallward had ever met and, if they had, what each had thought of the other.

‘Leave me now,’ said a stern voice behind him.

He turned and hurried out, barely noticing that the dead man had been pushed back into the chair, and that Campbell was staring into a shiny yellow face. As Dorian went downstairs, he heard the key turn in the lock.

It was well past seven when Campbell returned to the library. He looked pale, but completely calm. ‘I have done what you asked,’ he muttered.

They were her whole life, more precious than a place made sacred by love, more precious than anything else on earth. The boys greeted the news of our departure with childish delight. Clara asked whether we were going to Athens. ‘Perhaps,’ I answered, and her face lit up with pleasure. There she could see her parents’ tomb and the land filled with memories of her father’s glory. She had thought about those places constantly, though she never spoke of them. Remembering them had changed her childhood cheerfulness into seriousness and filled her mind with lofty, restless thoughts.

We also had dear friends, however humble, whom we could not leave behind. There was the lively, obedient horse Lord Raymond had given his daughter, Alfred’s dog, and a pet eagle whose eyesight had weakened with age. Yet we could not list the beloved creatures coming with us without grieving over our terrible losses and sighing deeply for everything we had to leave. Tears filled Idris’s eyes as Alfred and Evelyn brought first a favourite rose tree, then a beautifully carved marble vase, insisting that these must come too. They cried out at the pity of being unable to bring the castle and the forest, the deer and birds, and every familiar, treasured thing. ‘My affectionate, foolish children,’ I said, ‘we have already lost forever treasures far greater than these. We leave these things to save treasures beside which they are worth nothing. Let us always remember our purpose and our hope. They will hold back the flood of grief we feel over lesser things.’

The children were easily distracted and soon returned to thinking about the pleasures ahead. Idris had vanished. She had gone away to conceal her weakness, leaving the castle and walking down to the little park to find a place where she could weep alone. I found her with her arms around an old oak, pressing her rosy lips to its rough trunk. Tears poured down her face, and she could not hold back her sobs and broken cries. It hurt me beyond words to see the woman I loved so lost in sorrow. I drew her close. As she felt my kisses on her eyelids and my arms holding her, she became aware again of all she still had. ‘You are very kind not to blame me,’ she said. ‘I weep because a bitter, unbearable sorrow is tearing at my heart. Yet I am happy. Other mothers mourn their children, other wives lose their husbands, while you and my children are still here with me.’

About ten minutes later the tea bell rang. When Virginia failed to come downstairs, Mrs. Otis sent a footman to fetch her. He returned after a while and said he could not find Miss Virginia anywhere. Virginia usually went into the garden each evening to gather flowers for the dinner table, so at first her mother felt no concern. But when six o’clock struck and she still had not appeared, Mrs. Otis grew seriously worried. She sent the boys to look outside while she and Mr. Otis searched every room in the house. At half past six the boys returned without finding any sign of their sister. Everyone was now terribly anxious and at a loss about what to do. Then Mr. Otis remembered that a few days earlier he had allowed a group of gypsies to camp in the park. He immediately set out for Blackfell Hollow, where he knew they had been staying, taking his eldest son and two farm workers. The young Duke of Cheshire, frantic with worry, begged to join them, but Mr. Otis refused because he feared there might be a fight. When they reached the place, however, the campers had left. They seemed to have gone in a hurry: their fire was still burning, and plates lay on the grass. Mr. Otis sent Washington and the two men to search the surrounding area, then ran home. He dispatched telegrams to every police inspector in the county, asking them to watch for a young girl kidnapped by tramps or gypsies. Next he ordered his horse brought to the door. After insisting that his wife and the three boys sit down to dinner, he rode along the Ascot Road with a groom. He had scarcely travelled two miles when he heard someone galloping behind him. Looking back, he saw the little Duke approaching on his pony, bareheaded and red in the face. ‘I’m terribly sorry, Mr. Otis,’ the boy gasped, ‘but I can’t eat dinner while Virginia is missing. Please don’t be angry. If you had let us get engaged last year, none of this trouble would have happened. You won’t send me home, will you? I can’t go! I won’t!’

The Minister could not help smiling at the handsome young rascal, and Virginia’s devoted admirer touched him deeply. Leaning down from his horse, he patted the boy kindly on the shoulders. ‘Well, Cecil,’ he said, ‘if you refuse to go back, I suppose you must come with me. But I shall have to find you a hat in Ascot.’
